claim: Microglia account for 10% to 15% of all cells within the CNS.
source: Microglia are a unique population of tissue resident macrophages residing in the central nervous system (CNS) accounting for 10% to 15% of all cells within the CNS.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the introduction without specific citation, drawing from general scientific knowledge about microglia.

claim: Microglia display canonical macrophage activities such as phagocytosis of debris and apoptotic bodies.
source: While displaying some canonical macrophage activities such as the phagocytosis of debris and apoptotic bodies (Chan et al., 2001; Janda et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chan et al., 2001 and Janda et al., 2018.

claim: Microglia are endowed with CNS-specific functions including synaptic remodeling.
source: microglia are also endowed with functions specific to the CNS microenvironment (Clayton et al., 2017; Li and Barres, 2018; Ransohoff, 2016; Ransohoff and Khoury, 2016), such as synaptic remodeling (Paolicelli et al., 2011; Stephan et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007; Weinhard et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Paolicelli et al., 2011; Stephan et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007; Weinhard et al., 2018.

claim: Microglia provide neuronal support.
source: microglia are also endowed with functions specific to the CNS microenvironment (Clayton et al., 2017; Li and Barres, 2018; Ransohoff, 2016; Ransohoff and Khoury, 2016), such as synaptic remodeling (Paolicelli et al., 2011; Stephan et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007; Weinhard et al., 2018), neuronal support (Parkhurst et al., 2013; Ueno et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Parkhurst et al., 2013 and Ueno et al., 2013.

claim: Microglia are involved in oligodendrogenesis.
source: microglia are also endowed with functions specific to the CNS microenvironment (Clayton et al., 2017; Li and Barres, 2018; Ransohoff, 2016; Ransohoff and Khoury, 2016), such as synaptic remodeling (Paolicelli et al., 2011; Stephan et al., 2012; Stevens et al., 2007; Weinhard et al., 2018), neuronal support (Parkhurst et al., 2013; Ueno et al., 2013), and oligodendrogenesis (Hagemeyer et al., 2017; Wlodarczyk et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hagemeyer et al., 2017 and Wlodarczyk et al., 2017.

claim: No durable subsets of microglia have been identified in the healthy adult brain at steady-state.
source: However, despite this diversity of functions, no durable subsets have been identified in the healthy adult brain at steady-state.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the introduction, representing the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: Disease-associated microglia (DAM) arise in response to β-amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's Disease transgenic mouse models.
source: The disease-associated microglia (DAM) and the closely-related microglia subset expressing a neurodegenerative phenotype (MGnD) were reported to arise in response to the accumulation of β-amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) transgenic mouse models (Kamphuis et al., 2016; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Krasemann et al., 2017; Mrdjen et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kamphuis et al., 2016; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Krasemann et al., 2017; Mrdjen et al., 2018.

claim: DAM and MGnD subsets are found in models of neurodegeneration and aging.
source: The disease-associated microglia (DAM) and the closely-related microglia subset expressing a neurodegenerative phenotype (MGnD) were reported to arise in response to the accumulation of β-amyloid plaques in Alzheimer's Disease (AD) transgenic mouse models (Kamphuis et al., 2016; Keren-Shaul et al., 2017; Krasemann et al., 2017; Mrdjen et al., 2018), as well as in other models of neurodegeneration and aging (Chiu et al., 2013; Holtman et al., 2015; Spiller et al., 2018; Wlodarczyk et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chiu et al., 2013; Holtman et al., 2015; Spiller et al., 2018; Wlodarczyk et al., 2014.

claim: Proliferative-region-associated microglia (PAM) are associated with phagocytosis of newly formed and dying oligodendrocytes during normal post-natal development.
source: Mirroring the gene signature and function of DAM and MGnD subsets in disease conditions, the proliferative-region-associated microglia (PAM) subset was associated with the phagocytosis of newly formed and dying oligodendrocytes during normal post-natal development (Felsky et al., 2019; Hagemeyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Felsky et al., 2019; Hagemeyer et al., 2017; Li et al., 2019.

claim: Dark microglia are characterized by condensed, electron-dense cytoplasm visible by transmission electron microscopy.
source: Dark microglia, a subset identified by their condensed, electron-dense cytoplasm visible by transmission electron microscopy, are frequently observed during pathologic states and believed to actively associate with neuronal synapses (Bisht et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bisht et al., 2016.

claim: Dark microglia are frequently observed during pathologic states.
source: Dark microglia, a subset identified by their condensed, electron-dense cytoplasm visible by transmission electron microscopy, are frequently observed during pathologic states and believed to actively associate with neuronal synapses (Bisht et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bisht et al., 2016.

claim: Dark microglia are believed to actively associate with neuronal synapses.
source: Dark microglia, a subset identified by their condensed, electron-dense cytoplasm visible by transmission electron microscopy, are frequently observed during pathologic states and believed to actively associate with neuronal synapses (Bisht et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bisht et al., 2016 and is characterized as a belief, indicating some uncertainty.

claim: Regional variations in microglia cellular density exist in the adult steady-state CNS.
source: In particular, regional variations in cellular density (Lawson et al., 1990), but also in microglia gene expression profiles were reported, pointing to region-specific microglia functions and possibly subsets in healthy brain (Ayata et al., 2018; Grabert et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lawson et al., 1990.

claim: Regional variations in microglia gene expression profiles exist in the adult steady-state CNS.
source: In particular, regional variations in cellular density (Lawson et al., 1990), but also in microglia gene expression profiles were reported, pointing to region-specific microglia functions and possibly subsets in healthy brain (Ayata et al., 2018; Grabert et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ayata et al., 2018 and Grabert et al., 2016.

claim: Regional variations in microglia gene expression point to region-specific microglia functions.
source: In particular, regional variations in cellular density (Lawson et al., 1990), but also in microglia gene expression profiles were reported, pointing to region-specific microglia functions and possibly subsets in healthy brain (Ayata et al., 2018; Grabert et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited studies about regional variations.

claim: CD45dimCD11B+ microglia isolated from 6-month-old naïve C57BL/6 mice display a bimodal distribution of autofluorescence intensity.
source: Doing so revealed an unexpected bimodal distribution of autofluorescence (AF) intensity in CD45dimCD11B+ microglia isolated from 6-month-old naïve C57BL/6 mice (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The bimodal autofluorescence distribution identifies two subsets of microglia: AF-positive (AF+) and AF-negative (AF−).
source: This bimodal distribution identified two subsets of microglia: an AF-positive (AF+) subset showing a strong AF signal, and an AF-negative (AF−) subset which displayed no or minimal levels of AF.
evidence: This is a direct interpretation of the bimodal distribution observed in the data.

claim: The ratio of AF− to AF+ microglia is approximately 1:2.5.
source: The two subsets appeared at a highly reproducible ratio of 1:2.5 (AF−:AF+), with an average frequency of AF+ microglia of 71 ± 1.2% (n = 13; CV = 1.6%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from n=13 animals shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The average frequency of AF+ microglia is 71 ± 1.2% with a coefficient of variation of 1.6%.
source: The two subsets appeared at a highly reproducible ratio of 1:2.5 (AF−:AF+), with an average frequency of AF+ microglia of 71 ± 1.2% (n = 13; CV = 1.6%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from n=13 animals shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The AF signal shows maximal intensity in the 660–735 nm emission range upon excitation with a 488 nm laser.
source: The AF signal showed maximal intensity in the 660–735 nm emission range upon excitation with a 488 nm (Blue) laser but was also detected across multiple combinations of laser excitation wavelengths and emission filter ranges (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The AF signal is detected across multiple combinations of laser excitation wavelengths and emission filter ranges.
source: The AF signal showed maximal intensity in the 660–735 nm emission range upon excitation with a 488 nm (Blue) laser but was also detected across multiple combinations of laser excitation wavelengths and emission filter ranges (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The majority of microglia that are positive or negative for AF in the Blue-710 nm channel are also positive or negative across most other AF channels tested.
source: Extraction of single cell-level data from flow cytometry analyses revealed that the majority of microglia that were either positive or negative for AF in the Blue-710 nm AF channel were also positive or negative across most other AF channels tested, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell analysis data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Both AF+ and AF− microglia subsets are positive for microglia homeostatic markers including CX3CR1, P2RY12 and TMEM119.
source: Both AF+ and AF− subsets of microglia were positive for microglia homeostatic markers, including CX3CR1, P2RY12 and TMEM119 (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: There are no gender differences in the frequency of AF+ microglia.
source: Finally, there were no gender differences observed in the frequency of AF+ microglia nor the intensity of AF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: There are no gender differences in the intensity of AF in microglia.
source: Finally, there were no gender differences observed in the frequency of AF+ microglia nor the intensity of AF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Microglia isolated from 3- to 4-year-old Cynomolgus monkeys show a bimodal pattern of AF with an average of 80 ± 3.6% AF+ cells.
source: This observation was conserved across species as microglia isolated from the brains of 3- to 4-year-old Cynomolgus monkeys showed a very consistent bimodal pattern of AF in the Blue-710 nm channel with 80 ± 3.6% of microglia that were AF+ on average (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from non-human primates shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: The bimodal autofluorescence pattern in microglia is conserved between rodents and non-human primates.
source: This observation was conserved across species as microglia isolated from the brains of 3- to 4-year-old Cynomolgus monkeys showed a very consistent bimodal pattern of AF in the Blue-710 nm channel with 80 ± 3.6% of microglia that were AF+ on average (Figure 1E,F).
evidence: This is an inference based on observing similar patterns in both mice and non-human primates.

claim: The AF signal in AF+ microglia is punctate and localized within intracellular organelles.
source: Microscopy images of AF+ cells identified by the fluorescence intensity detected in two empty channels (Figure 1G) revealed that the AF signal was not diffusely distributed throughout the cellular volume but was punctate and localized within intracellular organelles.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The subcellular AF compartments are observed in all tested AF channels and systematically colocalize.
source: The subcellular AF compartments were observed in all tested AF channels and systematically colocalized (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I).
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and I.

claim: AF− cells do not display detectable AF subcellular compartments in any of the tested channels.
source: AF− cells did not display detectable AF subcellular compartments in any of the tested channels
evidence: This is based on imaging flow cytometry observations.

claim: AF subcellular structures become largely confluent in 10-month-old animals compared to the punctate signal in 3-month-old animals.
source: In contrast to the punctate AF signal detected in 3-month-old animals, imaging flow cytometry applied to naïve mice from a range of ages revealed that AF subcellular structures became largely confluent in 10-month-old animals and occupied a larger fraction of the cytosol (from 11 μm2 to 17 μm2 on average in 3- and 10- month-old animals, respectively) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: AF subcellular structures occupy a larger fraction of the cytosol with age, increasing from 11 μm2 to 17 μm2 on average between 3- and 10-month-old animals.
source: In contrast to the punctate AF signal detected in 3-month-old animals, imaging flow cytometry applied to naïve mice from a range of ages revealed that AF subcellular structures became largely confluent in 10-month-old animals and occupied a larger fraction of the cytosol (from 11 μm2 to 17 μm2 on average in 3- and 10- month-old animals, respectively) (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: AF signal intensity in AF+ microglia increases nearly linearly with aging.
source: Consistent with these results, flow cytometry analyses established a nearly linear increase of AF signal intensity in AF+ microglia with aging (Figure 2C,D)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data across multiple ages shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: AF signal intensity in AF+ microglia shows a cumulative 3-fold increase between 3- and 12-month-old mice across multiple fluorescence channels.
source: Consistent with these results, flow cytometry analyses established a nearly linear increase of AF signal intensity in AF+ microglia with aging (Figure 2C,D), resulting in a cumulative 3-fold increase of AF signal between 3- and 12-month-old mice across multiple fluorescence channels (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A clear AF+ population is not detectable in mice aged 15 days post-natal or younger.
source: While a clear AF+ population was not detectable in mice aged 15 days post-natal or younger, a bimodal distribution appeared as early as 30 days post-natal and AF increased linearly with age from that point on (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: A bimodal AF distribution appears as early as 30 days post-natal in mice.
source: While a clear AF+ population was not detectable in mice aged 15 days post-natal or younger, a bimodal distribution appeared as early as 30 days post-natal and AF increased linearly with age from that point on (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: AF increases linearly with age from 30 days post-natal onwards.
source: While a clear AF+ population was not detectable in mice aged 15 days post-natal or younger, a bimodal distribution appeared as early as 30 days post-natal and AF increased linearly with age from that point on (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by developmental time course data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Age-dependent increases in cellular AF are not detected in peripheral CD11B+ cells residing in the spleen.
source: In contrast, age-dependent increases in cellular AF were not detected in peripheral CD11B+ cells residing in the spleen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative data from spleen cells shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The frequency of AF+ microglia remains largely unchanged during aging, decreasing only slightly from 75% to 72% from 3 to 12 months of age.
source: Despite the large increase in the AF signal observed in AF+ cells, their frequency remained largely unchanged during aging, decreasing only slightly from 75% to 72% from 3 to 12 months of age (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The proportion of AF− cells is not altered by aging.
source: Finally, neither the proportion of AF− cells (Figure 2E) nor the area of intracellular AF signal detected in AF− microglia (Figure 2A,B) were altered by aging
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The area of intracellular AF signal detected in AF− microglia is not altered by aging.
source: Finally, neither the proportion of AF− cells (Figure 2E) nor the area of intracellular AF signal detected in AF− microglia (Figure 2A,B) were altered by aging
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Aging selectively impacts the AF+ microglia subset.
source: Finally, neither the proportion of AF− cells (Figure 2E) nor the area of intracellular AF signal detected in AF− microglia (Figure 2A,B) were altered by aging, revealing a selective impact of aging on the AF+ microglia subset.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that only AF+ cells show age-related changes.

claim: At 3 months of age, 80% of AF+ microglia contain large storage bodies filled with osmophilic electron-dense deposits.
source: At 3 months of age, the intracellular organization of AF microglia subsets differed in that AF+ cells almost systematically contained large storage bodies filled with osmophilic electron-dense deposits (Figure 3A). These electron-dense storage bodies were observed in 80% of AF+ microglia
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 3 months of age, only 46% of AF− microglia contain electron-dense organelles.
source: These electron-dense storage bodies were observed in 80% of AF+ microglia whereas only 46% of AF− microglia contained electron-dense organelles (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: Storage bodies in AF− cells are devoid of complex storage material and are more regularly shaped than those in AF+ cells.
source: When observed in AF− cells, storage bodies were devoid of complex storage material and were more regularly shaped than those observed in AF+ cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Between 3 and 18 months of age, the percentage of visible cytoplasm occupied by storage bodies in AF+ microglia increases from 9% to 23% on average.
source: Between 3 and 18 months of age, the percentage of visible cytoplasm occupied by storage bodies increased from 9% to 23% on average
evidence: This is based on quantitative TEM analysis.

claim: Approximately 30% of AF+ cells from aged mice contain AF material that occupies more than a third of the cytoplasm.
source: Between 3 and 18 months of age, the percentage of visible cytoplasm occupied by storage bodies increased from 9% to 23% on average and approximately 30% of AF+ cells from aged mice contained AF material that occupied more than a third of the cytoplasm (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative TEM data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ultrastructural composition of storage bodies in AF+ cells includes curvilinear and fingerprint-like profiles.
source: The ultrastructural composition of the storage bodies in AF+ cells varied with frequent curvilinear (black arrowheads) and fingerprint-like profiles (red arrowheads) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM images shown in Figure 3B.

claim: White, linear, rod-like material with fine-tipped ends observed in AF+ cells closely resemble cholesterol crystal deposits.
source: White, linear, rod-like material with fine-tipped ends (white arrowheads) were observed within membrane-bound lipoid bodies and closely resembled cholesterol crystal deposits (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an inference based on morphological similarity observed in TEM images shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lipid droplets are the most prominent component of storage bodies in AF+ microglia.
source: Most prominent, however, was the proportion and volume of lipid droplets (asterisks) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM observations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The frequency of AF− cells containing storage bodies remains unchanged with aging.
source: In contrast, both the frequency of cells containing storage bodies and the proportion of the cytosol occupied by storage bodies remained unchanged in the AF− microglia subset (Figure 3A,C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3A,C,D.

claim: The proportion of cytosol occupied by storage bodies in AF− microglia remains unchanged with aging.
source: In contrast, both the frequency of cells containing storage bodies and the proportion of the cytosol occupied by storage bodies remained unchanged in the AF− microglia subset (Figure 3A,C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3A,C,D.

claim: AF+ cells express higher levels of LAMP1 compared to AF− cells.
source: In addition to these ultrastructural differences, AF+ cells expressed higher levels of LAMP1 and CD68 compared to AF− cells (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: AF+ cells express higher levels of CD68 compared to AF− cells.
source: In addition to these ultrastructural differences, AF+ cells expressed higher levels of LAMP1 and CD68 compared to AF− cells (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: Higher LAMP1 and CD68 levels in AF+ cells indicate an enlargement of endolysosomal storage compartments.
source: In addition to these ultrastructural differences, AF+ cells expressed higher levels of LAMP1 and CD68 compared to AF− cells (Figure 3E,F), indicating an enlargement of endolysosomal storage compartments in AF+ cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known functions of LAMP1 and CD68 as endolysosomal markers.

claim: LAMP1 protein levels show a gradual age-dependent increase in the AF+ subset.
source: Furthermore, a gradual age-dependent increase in LAMP1 and CD68 protein levels was observed in the AF+ subset (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data across ages shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: CD68 protein levels show a gradual age-dependent increase in the AF+ subset.
source: Furthermore, a gradual age-dependent increase in LAMP1 and CD68 protein levels was observed in the AF+ subset (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data across ages shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: AF− microglia do not show age-dependent changes in LAMP1 and CD68 levels.
source: Furthermore, a gradual age-dependent increase in LAMP1 and CD68 protein levels was observed in the AF+ subset (Figure 3E,F) whereas AF− microglia did not show changes.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: AF+ microglia differ from AF− cells by their unique accumulation of endolysosomal storage compartments with aging.
source: Altogether these observations indicated that AF+ microglia differed from AF− cells by their unique accumulation of endolysosomal storage compartments with aging.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the combined TEM and flow cytometry data.

claim: BLZ945 treatment results in nearly complete microglia depletion 24 hours after treatment.
source: Twenty-four hours following the treatment period, depletion was nearly complete, as assessed by the remaining frequency and absolute numbers of microglia (Figure 4A,B and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Microglia rapidly repopulate the CNS at 7 and 14 days post-BLZ945 treatment.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Huang et al., 2018; O'Neil et al., 2018), microglia rapidly repopulated the CNS at 7 and 14 days post-treatment, recovering on average to 25% (at 7 days) and 87% (at 14 days) of steady-state microglia numbers (Figure 4A and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: AF− microglia reach 67% of steady-state levels by day 7 post-depletion.
source: While AF− microglia cell numbers reached 67% of steady-state levels by day 7, AF+ cells only repopulated to 4% of steady-state levels by that time (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AF+ microglia only repopulate to 4% of steady-state levels by day 7 post-depletion.
source: While AF− microglia cell numbers reached 67% of steady-state levels by day 7, AF+ cells only repopulated to 4% of steady-state levels by that time (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: At 14 days post-depletion, repopulating AF+ cells reach only 14% of steady-state values while AF− cells surpass steady-state levels by approximately 2-fold.
source: At 14 days repopulating AF+ cell numbers only reached 14% of steady-state AF+ values in vehicle-treated mice while the repopulating AF− subset surpassed steady-state levels by approximately 2-fold (Figure 4B)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: AF− microglia normalize to steady-state levels by day 70 post-depletion.
source: At 14 days repopulating AF+ cell numbers only reached 14% of steady-state AF+ values in vehicle-treated mice while the repopulating AF− subset surpassed steady-state levels by approximately 2-fold (Figure 4B) before normalizing to steady-state levels at day 70.
evidence: This is stated in the text based on the repopulation kinetics data.

claim: The AF− subset is the first subset to repopulate the depleted brain.
source: Altogether these results established that the AF− subset was the first subset to repopulate the depleted brain while the repopulation by AF+ cells was delayed
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential repopulation kinetics observed.

claim: The delayed repopulation by AF+ cells suggests a possible conversion from AF− to AF+ state during repopulation.
source: Altogether these results established that the AF− subset was the first subset to repopulate the depleted brain while the repopulation by AF+ cells was delayed, suggesting a possible conversion from AF− to AF+ state during repopulation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the repopulation kinetics.

claim: The AF intensity of repopulated microglia slowly increases from barely detectable levels at day 7 to slightly increased levels at day 14.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the AF intensity of the repopulated microglia slowly increased from barely detectable levels at day seven to slightly increased levels at day 14, ultimately returning to a bimodal distribution by day 70 (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Repopulated microglia return to a bimodal AF distribution by day 70 post-depletion.
source: Supporting this hypothesis, the AF intensity of the repopulated microglia slowly increased from barely detectable levels at day seven to slightly increased levels at day 14, ultimately returning to a bimodal distribution by day 70 (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: At day 70 post-depletion, only 19% of the newly-formed AF+ subset displays AF intensity levels comparable to vehicle-treated mice.
source: Even at the latter timepoint, only a small fraction of this newly-formed AF+ subset (19% on average) displayed AF intensity levels comparable to those seen in vehicle-treated mice (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B)
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Most repopulating AF+ cells at day 70 display 35% weaker AF signal intensity on average compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: Even at the latter timepoint, only a small fraction of this newly-formed AF+ subset (19% on average) displayed AF intensity levels comparable to those seen in vehicle-treated mice (Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B) while most repopulating AF+ cells displayed 35% weaker AF signal intensity on average.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The gradual accumulation of AF material over time in repopulating microglia supports the possibility that AF+ microglia are derived from conversion of AF− cells.
source: This gradual accumulation of AF material over time in repopulating microglia supported the possibility that AF+ microglia were derived from the conversion of AF− cells during replenishment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics of AF accumulation during repopulation.

claim: 56% of microglia display positivity for KI-67 at day 7 post-depletion.
source: Further validating this conclusion, 56% of microglia displayed positivity for the proliferation-associated marker KI-67 at day seven before returning to steady-state values by day 14 (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: KI-67 positivity returns to steady-state values by day 14 post-depletion.
source: Further validating this conclusion, 56% of microglia displayed positivity for the proliferation-associated marker KI-67 at day seven before returning to steady-state values by day 14 (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4E,F.

claim: AF+ microglia are virtually absent during the early repopulation phase at day 7.
source: Because AF+ microglia were virtually absent during this early repopulation phase (Figure 4B), these proliferation kinetics implied that the AF− subset of microglia was the predominant subset responsible for the repopulation of the microglia compartment following depletion
evidence: This is based on the quantitative data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The AF− subset of microglia is the predominant subset responsible for repopulation following depletion.
source: Because AF+ microglia were virtually absent during this early repopulation phase (Figure 4B), these proliferation kinetics implied that the AF− subset of microglia was the predominant subset responsible for the repopulation of the microglia compartment following depletion
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined proliferation and subset frequency data.

claim: AF+ microglia are derived from the conversion over time of a subset of AF− microglia.
source: Because AF+ microglia were virtually absent during this early repopulation phase (Figure 4B), these proliferation kinetics implied that the AF− subset of microglia was the predominant subset responsible for the repopulation of the microglia compartment following depletion and that AF+ microglia were derived from the conversion over time of a subset of AF− microglia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the repopulation kinetics and AF accumulation dynamics.

claim: A total of 4231 proteins were detected by label-free LC-MS/MS in FACS-isolated AF+ and AF− microglia.
source: A total of 4231 proteins were detected by label-free LC-MS/MS and after filtering for proteins quantified in at least 50% of samples in either subset, 3492 remained for analysis.
evidence: This is a direct report of the proteomic analysis results.

claim: 351 proteins show significant differences in abundance between AF+ and AF− microglia.
source: 351 proteins showed significant differences in abundance between AF+ and AF− microglia (Benjamini-Hochberg adj. p value < 0.01, fold-change > |1.3|), with 254 and 97 upregulated and downregulated differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), respectively (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: 254 proteins are upregulated in AF+ microglia compared to AF− microglia.
source: 351 proteins showed significant differences in abundance between AF+ and AF− microglia (Benjamini-Hochberg adj. p value < 0.01, fold-change > |1.3|), with 254 and 97 upregulated and downregulated differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), respectively (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: 97 proteins are downregulated in AF+ microglia compared to AF− microglia.
source: 351 proteins showed significant differences in abundance between AF+ and AF− microglia (Benjamini-Hochberg adj. p value < 0.01, fold-change > |1.3|), with 254 and 97 upregulated and downregulated differentially expressed proteins (DEPs), respectively (Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: 32 of the top 50 DEPs upregulated in AF+ microglia are associated with endolysosomal biology.
